newsitem.title: UK: Copper wanes in late LME trade, finishes lower.
newsitem.headline: Copper wanes in late LME trade, finishes lower.

text.p: Copper prices turned lower during Tuesday afternoon LME trading, depressed by disappointed liquidation, and the market ended an undramatic session lower.

Traders said the main catalyst for the trend was a smaller than expected warehouse stock fall of 2,525 tonnes. Although inventories are at fresh six-year lows, and there were no deliveries into Singapore the market is unconvinced.

"People were calling it (stocks) down by 5,000 to 7,000 tonnes, so when the decline came in lower it (the market) lost its way. I do not think we will see much now, with options on Wednesday," one said.
The selling in the afternoon put prices back below $1,970, and left chartists favouring the downside if there are no surprises in Wednesday's November option declarations.
There is also the perception that the run of stock drawdowns could be coming to an end soon, with metal expected to accumulate in Singapore that was shipped from Europe.
Additionally, deliveries in Northern European warehouses may well be Chinese metal, which suggest that recent liftings by China may not be for consumption.
Last three months business was at $1,961 a tonne, a $11 loss from Monday's kerb.
The cash/threes backwardation narrowed marginally to $40/43 on Tuesday.
Elsewhere in the base metals complex movements largely mirrored copper, traders noted.
"When things are as quiet as they are at present, copper tends to lead the way, and today was no exception," one said.

However, aluminium proved resilient to the downturn in copper, as the market capitalised on early short-covering, as well as some protective buying ahead of Wednesday's options declarations which was designed to keep downside puts out of play.
The market was also aided by the 3,425-tonne drop in stocks, and final kerb trade was at $1,432, a $7.50 gain from Monday.

Nickel's earlier rally was aborted in mid-afternoon, with prices drifting back in line with copper. The 720-tonne stock increase was also inhibitive, and by the end of the kerb the market was back at $7,150, down $10 from Monday.
Zinc's fortunes mostly matched copper, although the market has lost much of last week's upside momentum. The 850-tonne drop in inventories was marginally supportive, but somewhat small-scale.
Chart-based buying prevented the market from sliding under $1,060, and last business was at $1,062.50, down $3.50 from Monday.
Lead interest was slow throughout the session, and a modest 400-tonne decline in stocks merely underlined the uninspiring trend. Final business in a narrowly traded market was at $744, up $3.
Both thse markets will be keeping a cautious eye on developments at Noranda's Heath Steel lead and zinc mine in New Brunswick, where production has been halted after an explosion on Monday.

Tin staged a half-hearted rally after earlier equalling Monday's 17-month lows, but struggled to make any headway above $5,900, despite a 145-tonne fall in stocks. Last trade was at $5,905, up just $5 from yesterday.
Scant interest was seen in the alloy contract, although three months finished at a steadier $1,285/90, up from Monday's $1,278, helped by constructive charts.
--Martin Hayes, London newsroom 44 171 542 8080
